I am 63 years old and have been farming these fields in Quzhou for over forty years. My family has about 7 mu of good flat land on the North China Plain. Every year, I follow the same rotation that my neighbors and I have always used: winter wheat followed by summer maize. I don't take risks with new crops like vegetables or cotton at my age — the wheat and maize double-cropping system gives me stable yields and I know there are buyers for both.

The wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October. Now it is April and the wheat is greening up after winter dormancy. I will topdress it with urea (about 55 kg of nitrogen per mu) and irrigate it three times before harvest in early June. I don't bother buying phosphate or potash fertilizers — they cost too much and my wheat has always grown fine without them. I use an improved wheat variety like Jimai 22 because the seed shop in town sells it and it gives reliable yields around 1000 kg per mu. For tillage, I already rotary-tilled before sowing the wheat last autumn.

After I harvest the wheat in June, I will immediately sow summer maize, likely Denghai 605 hybrid seed. I won't till the soil — I will plant directly into the wheat stubble to save time, diesel, and my own labor. The leftover nitrogen from the wheat fertilization is enough for the maize, so I won't apply more fertilizer to the maize crop. I will irrigate the maize twice and spray pesticides three times to control insects and weeds. By October, I expect about 1050 kg per mu of maize.

This rotation is what I know, what my body can still manage, and what keeps food on the table.
